projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Earl Mahl was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: In Elyria here.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: In Elyria here?

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: I just lived in a suburb here,and I was drafted out of the North Ridgefield draft board. In fact, they give me a one-month extension because my wife was pregnant with a baby and they let -- I was supposed to go in June and I didn't go until July. They let me stay home that one month until the baby was born in June. And then I went in June to Cleveland and then I was inducted into Cleveland and went to basic training at Fort Bragg, North -- well, we first went to Columbus.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was this '42?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: '43. Okay.

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: July of' 43. I went in and actually went to active duty in August of '43 to Columbus to Fort Hayes, where most everybody went, I think. And then from Fort Hayes -- I guess a need was at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, because there was a whole trainload from all over the country in the training center at Fort Bragg, North Carolina. And we trained there on 105 Howitzers, which I thought was a great gun. But one day we come out of the mess hall and they had a scale set up there and a height chart. Well, we knew they had that some place, but they were doing it all over again. But later on, we found out that everybody over 5'8" and a 175 pounds went to the mule pack, because they wanted bigger people for handling the mules. 'Cause the pack saddle itself weighed 90 pounds. And normally what you would do is two people would pick up a pack saddle and walk over to the back of a mule and set it down on a mule's back. Well, that was stateside procedure. When we got overseas, you'd grab a pack saddle and throw it on a mule's back and when he's still trying to catch his breath, you'd grab the cinches and pull them up and you're -- each guy would pack their own mules. You know, we had -- while we were in action, I got assigned to C Battery of 613. I was in the headquarters of supply. And they broke everything down at headquarters and sent them out to gun batteries. And I went to C Battery of 613 and just hauled ammunition and supplies for them with four other people, and, I think, 15 mules we had for packing. We just hauled for C Battery.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So can you tell me anything more about that training when you got assigned to that outfit stateside?

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: Well, I thought the 105 was a great thing. And I had a truck driver's license, so I got to drive a truck down there some, and I thought that was going to be great. And the 105 Howitzer was a great gun. I just thought you could pull into a place and -- I know with training with the 105s, we'd go out in the field and we'd have training sessions and they'd see how many shells they could have in the air before the first one landed. It was a challenge. You know, they'd have four, five shells in the air before the first one landed. The 75s weren't quite that -- they were quite fast, but not that -- you -- sort of an upright position with the 75 -- 105s and it was really handy to operate them. But I never got on a gun -- I never worked on a gun itself. I was -- got put in a supply section out in -- we went from Fort Bragg to Camp Gruber, Oklahoma. And I think that was only a place to get us started, because they -- we went there and were just incorporated, you might say. And then they bought the mules there and they bought -- all these were newly bought mules by the government. They buy them and take them to what they call a remount station. At the remount station, they give them all their shots and they give them also -- they brand them with identifications in their lip and on the back of their shoulder. And they pack them once. So we got a bunch of mules at Camp Gruber, Oklahoma, that were just about as wild as could be. And we had a lot of people in our outfit who had never saw a mule before. We had them from New York and Jersey and never saw -- I had seen mules. In fact, I worked with my uncle on a farm out here. I had plowed with a team of mules. But we got a mule to take back to the stables. And by the time we got done with that, there was mules all over that camp for a week until we finally gathered them all in and got them all back to where they were going. But it was -- the place was all new. And it rained and it was mud. We had mud all over everything. And we were only there -- I think we originated in December and we left there in February. They moved us all to Camp Carson, Colorado. And half of the batteries and battalions' people went ahead to accept the mules and the other half stayed behind and shipped them. So I was in the group to go ahead and to get them off the trains and I always remember one instance there. We -- naturally, we come in at 2 o'clock in the morning. And we went down the train and took them back the stables. We got back about 4:00, 4:30, something like that and got them done. And we weren't in bed five minutes, and the whistle blowed, the light goes on. Get up, go back and water the mules, you got to water them. So that was another thing you had to do. And with the mule pack, you had other duties besides KP. You had to pull a stable police and you'd clean the stables up and feed them and water them for the day if you weren't going take them out and pack them. But our training was all at Fort Carson and we went out in the hills there. We never got up in the mountains. Some organizations went up to the Pikes Peak, but we never went up to Pikes Peak. It was cold out there. I can remember some nights bivouac out there and you'd get down -- we had these feather tick sleeping bags and they were warm. You could -- of course, you get inside of one of them and zip the whole thing shut and then you didn't know how to get out of it. You know, that was always problem. But we completed our training there in around July or August. There were really four battalions originated. 6, 10, 11, 12, and 13. And then we -- in July sometime they came in there and did a training session and an evaluation on all the battalions. And they eliminated 610 and 611 and took a lot of people and put them in 612 and 613. But evidently that was the plan to eliminate some of these people and get the best two battalions they have. We -- 613 really had a higher rating, but 612 had a pretty aggressive commander and they wanted to have some group of people take a boat -- boatloads of mules over. So 612 volunteered for that and they went before 613 did. But they went to New Orleans and shipped out of New Orleans with mule. I think they had about 300 mules on that mule boat. I don't know if they had more than one mule boat going. But the mules we got overseas were all American mules, because they were a bigger animal than they had over in the other -- over there. And then we left out of Long Beach in November sometime.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This would be November of '44?

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: Yeah. November of '44. I know it was two days to go from Long Beach to Bombay, India. We stopped two days in Melbourne, Australia, to take on some supplies. They wouldn't let anybody off the docks. We could get off the boat, but we couldn't get off the dock because they were afraid they'd lose a few people, I think. Then we went into Bombay, and we really were the only combat unit on that ship, The General Buttoner [ph]. Most of the rest of the people on the boat were Air Force replacement. A lot -- mostly Chinese who could speak Chinese, American-Chinese. So we got on a train and we went from Bombay four days across to camp -- outside Calcutta called Camp Shapiro. And we thought, well, we'll get a little break here. And that wasn't to be. We met about 6 o'clock that night and they said if you want to get some sleep do it because the first plane pulls out for Myilkyima, Burma, at midnight. And by 6 o'clock the next night our whole unit was over in Burma already, up in Myilkyima. And we were only in Burma for a short time, just enough to get our supplies in. And I was with a group of -- in the supply section we went down and got a bunch of mules that they had at some corrals down there and brought them back for all of our units. In about 10, 15 days we were on our way to the front. And that map goes through where we went each day, each overnight stop down the way. And it was quite an experience. One day we -- we went down -- I think it was the Shweli River that we crossed. And it had rained. And we slid down the mountain most the way. And we got across the river. We went across a foot bridge and we pushed -- give the mules a kick in the rear end and they'd go through the water and we picked them up on the other side. The bridge wasn't heavy enough to face the mule. But then we got into a rainstorm for about three days and we were there and no planes could get in with supplies. We didn't have no food for about three days. But then the next morning they decided we're going to get out of that place and get up on top of a mountain some place. We could hear planes flying over, but they couldn't get to us. So we moved out of there. And that morning, I remember, I stayed back. And the planes had got in. It came up a clear morning and they throwed a bunch of rations out. And one thing I'll always remember. They dumped a bunch of fresh bread. Oh, my god, fresh bread. Where did it go? In the river. We dug it out and ate it, because -- I ended up with dysentery in the eventual end of the thing. But -- then I -- my experience was once we got to Nam Packa and got set up with our gun batteries, then I -- my time was spent mostly hauling supplies from the airdrop. It was a big valley where all the -- well, the first day I remember pulling up there. This valley must have had a thousand parachutes laying in it, all different colors. And each color was different item. You know, green was medics and red was the ammunition and so on. We changed it after awhile because the Japanese were getting the word of it. But I spent a lot of days hauling ammunition out of that airdrop. Back to the -- back to the gun battery, which we were in a valley on the back of a mountainside where we could lob the shells over the mountainside. And the only really close call I had was the Japanese started firing -- they had a 150 Howitzer they were firing on us. And they started firing into this airdrop and you could see they were starting down the other end and they were dropping -- they were zeroing in, coming closer and closer and closer as we got there. Finally, somebody said, Get out of here, they're going to hit us. And I remember it was lines of mules; we had a lot of supplies to haul. And I would back up against a mule right there. Well, I ran and crawled up in a hole on the hillside and there was a shell hit right -- I thought, boy, that was right where we were at. And I looked up and this mule that I was backed up against was bleeding -- must have been 15 spots and it had shrapnel, just shot it all up. And I look a few minutes later and the mule was down dead. But that was right in the airdrop. But once we -- the Air Force came in, then it took that gun out. And then we got down there and we packed those mules and we headed back to our units again. But it was interesting. As I say, my wife was home with my one child. And I was in the Army three years. When I -- we went from there -- after the -- we did finally get the Japanese out of there. They were very resistant. And finally the last push was to get them out. And we hauled ammunition for must have been two weeks, I think. We had it piled up six-, eight-foot high. We could haul 11 rounds on a mule. Three -- we had some clips that fastened on the saddles and it held three clover leafs and we'd tie one around each clover leaf. So we'd haul 11 rounds back, and you'd be leading one -- riding a mule and leading three mules, each with 11 rounds on a mule. So you held 33 rounds of a shot you could make. And just continuously hauling that stuff. But I remember the last push they made, they just could not get the Japanese out of there and we had hauled this ammunition. And they started at 6 in the -- normally during a fire mission, they would zero in with one of the four guns in a gun battery and then when they got in where the target was at, that battery would shoot maybe three or four rounds. It was very limited because, you know, all this ammunition had to be flown into us. But that morning started out, and they were starting out with 15 rounds. And they had all their guns preset. And after the 15 rounds, they would just cancel it out and they'd move their trajectories up a little bit on them and go another 15 rounds. And for two hours they kept firing like that. And, in fact, I talked to an infantry man after it was all other with and he said, We jumped out at 8 o'clock and there was nothing left. The infantry -- the military -- artillery had just wiped everything out. And so that was really about the last day. And they had convoys sitting there waiting for us to get this road opened up. And the next day, these convoys were rolling through there. And we only stayed there a couple three more days and then we went down to Lashio for a while. And then they decided to take the units to China. And most the people were flown to China. But by me being in the supply section with the mules, a bunch of us took the mules and walked them back on a Burma road back -- not the Burma Road but a road they built across Burma, to Myilkyima. And then they decided to take them to China. And so we walked them from China -- from Myilkyima to China, Kunming, China. And you see that map is -- that's -- and I got to drive a truck during that session. That's why I had the map. Because what we would do, I had a 6 by 6 with a trailer on behind and all the kitchen equipment was in the truck. And the trailer had all the blacksmith stuff. All the mules kept shoes on; we kept shoes on all the mules all the time. And we had a medic with us and a veterinarian. And what I'd do with the truck is that I'd take the medics -- I'd take the kitchen people and we'd drive to the next bivouac area and they would get the kitchen set up and the food made for supper. And then they'd bring the mules in, they'd put them on picket lines and have supper. And then go through the next day and they'd all pull out and we'd clean up the kitchen and move onto the next location. It was that way for almost two months. Let's see, we left here on the 30th of May, 1945, and I think we got into the China sometime in the end of July, I think, I don't know exactly. Then we were at this Hostel 9 in Kunming, which was like a camp in the States; they call them hostels over there. And they were preparing to send us out with the mules to the Chinese army and some of the units did go out. They were just four or five guys going out with the Chinese army with 75 or a 100 mules and they were there to see if the Chinese took care of the mules. And I was scheduled to go out, but then the war ended and those guys finally came back and I worked my way -- I had a few more points than the other fellas did. Most the unit people went to China, Shanghai. I went back to India and I came out of -- went back to the same camp I was at before that and got on a ship. I didn't tell I was -- I had dysentery until I got in the ship and it pulled away from the dock, because I didn't want to stay in the hospital over there. So I was in sick bay on the ship all the way back. And then I went back to sick bay at Camp Kilmer for a couple weeks. And then I went to a hospital at Fort Monmouth for awhile and then they took me to Halloran General Hospital in Staten Island for the last two or three months and finally got discharged in July or August of 1945.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you first went into action there, was that with the Mars task force?

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did "Mars" stand for?

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: Well, there's been a lot of suppositions. There was a guy named General Mars, and they don't know if it was named after him or others. They never have come up with exactly why. But there was always a lot of rumors going around that Tokyo Rose was saying, those guys must have come from Mars, they wouldn't have come across those mountains. Those mountains are too rough. But I'll tell you, it was rough going across those mountains. You're up and down and it's those maps -- you'll see on those maps, it's just a trail. It's just a trail. There's no other way of getting into those places. It's a trail in the jungle is what it was. But see we -- there were two infantry outfits, 124th Calvary, which was a Texas National Guard outfit, which we supported. The 613th supported the Texas National 124th; the 612 supported the old 475th which was the remnants of the Merrill's Marauders. And that's the two -- I guess they were regiments, infantry regiments.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And your mission was to open up the Burma Road?

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: Get the road opened up. This intersection where -- they had built this road across Burma -- to get this intersection opened up so that they could take -- they could drive trucks. Otherwise, up till that point all the trucks had to be dismantled and flown to China. And they had convoys sitting there. And those convoys passed us on the way to China. They had Negro trucking companies that drove these trucks. And all those with supplies and everything they needed and those guys were a bunch of cowboys. And they had trucking companies set up all along the Burma Road for those trucking companies to stay over night. They'd give them a meal and they got showers and the next morning they're on the road again. They wouldn't be over ten foot apart, those guys, and they just going. They only make a hundred miles a day, but up in the mountains, you're just -- you're going in low gear, you know, a lot times. 'Cause the Burma Road is just hardly a road. Just a little -- I always say it was like Cascade Park down here. It was a park that just had a road that wound around through the park. It was two lanes most of the way. You could pass if you got over a little bit. Not much of a road, but it had been built by the coolies and people like that. That was quite an experience.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any particularly close buddies over there, overseas?

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: Oh, yeah, yeah. When I went in to -- when I took -- four other people and me and we went to C Battery, we had three other people who got to be real close because one of them -- you always bunk two guys. One fella by the name of Coons [ph] was from -- he was from Pennsylvania. Then we had two fellas that were close friends from Mississippi, John Bailey [ph] and Jimmy Alexander. Jimmy Alexander was a barber; he carried a bunch of barber tools with him. And he cut everybody's hair. And those really were the closest people we had -- that I had -- right while we were in action. As we -- of course, I stayed with -- I was in the supply section and it seemed like that was -- those guys hung together, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get a chance to do anything to relieve the tension, anything during any of the breaks?

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: Well, we built a couple huts. I still have -- I remember us building a hut. We were going to be at this place for about a week and we would see these natives' huts, you know. And I was going -- we were going -- me and my buddies were going to build a hut. And the natives all had a bamboo floor in their huts. And so I was going to make a bamboo -- and I took -- bamboo is great to work with, if you've ever done anything with bamboo. You know, they're about this big around and they got all these sections in them, you know. And I tried to cut that thing apart and I couldn't do it for nothing. And a native was standing there watching me. I tried to force it open by pinching my fingers and he went and took his -- they have like a machete, like a meat cleaver, some of them had. And he went to each one of those seams and he cut all the way around them. And then he went to the next one. When he got down to the end of it, he went like this with his knife and that thing went like that and flopped open. Here I pinched my fingers all the time but just didn't think -- knowing how to do. I sent some baskets home, but my wife never got them. Somebody picked them up on the way, I guess. I bought some new baskets that the natives carried on their backs. But I sent a couple of them home. I sent -- I did send a bunch of parachute cloth home. My mother, she made quilts and stuff. That parachute cloth was good stuff. We used to line our foxhole; we lined our foxhole with that parachute cloth. There was thousands of parachutes, you know. But I lined my -- Ed Coons and I, we had -- we dug a hole in the side of the mountain and put logs across it. And then we'd decorated the inside with two parachutes and we lived in there for about three weeks, four weeks, I guess.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any close buddies over there?

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: Not really close to me. In our outfit, lost a total of about six or seven people in the 613. But I didn't close any lose buddies. My -- I do have an experience of -- we had a buddy from New Mexico named Delbert Long and he was a slow talking, New Mexico rancher. And he was a -- he drank a lot. Very much. He was a very heavy drinker. And he always got in trouble. And I always remember when we were in action there, he did something and got in trouble, so they took him up to the front to lead a mule for the forward observers. Well, the forward observers are right up with the infantry; in fact, in front of the infantry. And he came back one day a week or two later and he needed a shave, he was dirty and crummy. And I'll always remember how he talked so slow. And, of course, we always would kid him and say, well, Long, how you doing? He said, them sons of bitches were trying to get me killed, he says. He was -- incidents like that, you know. Quite an experience.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, I'm guessing you probably didn't, but I'll ask. How about mail call. Did you get any mail out there?

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You did get mail?

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: We got mail. In fact, I have pictures in my book of getting mail. Yeah, we got mail quite regularly. My folks -- in fact, my folks sent me a box pert near every week and I got it. Yeah, mail, sure.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What kinds of things were they able to send you in the packages?

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: Oh, candies and cookies and stuff like that to eat.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: And that's about -- my folks always sent me a box a week. What else can I help you with?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The mail. Did those come by airdrops?

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. I think there's a picture in here of mail call. Yeah, we got mail pretty good.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Very good. I guess they had to know where you were to drop the supplies?

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How often did those supply drops come?

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: Oh, god, these planes were in there pert near every day. Yeah, they were -- they never had no doors on them. Old C-46s and 47s with the doors off of them. And there was two different kinds of drops. You get -- all the parachute stuff came in with parachutes, medical, food, and ammunition. Then the -- we got supplies for the mules. Grain for the mules always come in three small bags and a larger bag and that was free dropped. Man, when they came down, it came down. And they'd drop about -- they'd kick out about -- they'd pile them up in the door and just as they got to this certain point, they'd push them all out. And they hit the ground like a ton of brick. But they were -- and they wouldn't break open unless they hit a limb or a tree or something like that. They would hold up pretty good. Three small bags and a larger bag.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any other stories that you remember from your time overseas? Any other vivid memories come to mind from that time?

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: Well, I can't think too much. Except at the very last -- I remember when the Japanese surrendered, I had just got a cholera shot that day and, man, that shot really hurts. And I was laying in bed just like -- my arm just felt like it was jumping. Finally the word come that the Japanese surrendered and that was the end of that. We were up all the rest of the night, I think, that night. They had these Chinese kids going -- bringing bottles of wine in and everything else. I remember an incident when I was driving these mules -- driving a truck to China, I had hauled some -- I had to haul some rations on the back of the truck for some reason. Grapefruit juice was a big thing they used to send overseas. Grapefruit juice. And I was -- I had two or three fellas I was supposed to haul some place, and I can't remember the reason for it. But the truck was piled pretty high with the grapefruit juice, and they didn't have too much room to sit in the back end there. There was one guy that was a heavy drinker. And he kept asking me to stop at some little community and get some saki. They wanted to get saki and mix it with this grapefruit juice. And so finally we went to a little community and I stopped and they went and got their canteens full of saki. And we started out again and I had to stop for some reason or other and I went back there and this guy was really wally eyed. And I said, be careful you don't fall out of the back of this truck. Well, it wasn't ten minutes after that I had a real steep climb to go up a mountain. I was down in the lowest gear in the truck. And a native come running up next to me and he's waving his hands and hollering. And he said to stop; you know, he was trying to communicate to me. And so I stopped and set the brakes and went back and here this guy is walking up the hillside. He had fell off that truck. I run over him with the trailer. His face was peeled, just skin all off of his face. I thought I killed him. He got back in the truck and we went on. I saw him a few days after that; his face was all scabs all over and everything. But if he hadn't been drunk he probably would have got killed. If he hadn't have been drunk, he'd have got killed.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember where you were when you heard the news about the atomic bomb?

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: Well, I was at the Hostel 9 'cause that ended the war quickly. I was at this Hostel 9 in Kunming.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any idea what that was when they said --

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: Well, we were hoping.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It just meant the end hopefully?

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: Yeah, we were hopeful. We had a lot of hopes, you know. Because I was already assigned to the Chinese regiment to go out with them and some of our fellas already left. And I wasn't too happy about going out with them. But then that stopped everything. As soon as they surrendered, why that stopped the going out with them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reunion with your family like when you finally got back to the States?

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: Oh, great. Yeah, well, I came -- I came on a train from Staten Island, New York central. And the trains are always run here. And, of course, I knew the trains. I worked in that station. My dad had worked in that railway station up there. It was quite a reunion. Of course, my wife came to see me in the hospital. She came on -- she came when I was at Fort Monmouth. She came there and my folks came with her. And I think she came twice, I think. Once my folks came with her and once she came up by train, I think. It was great when the trains were operating. Now there's -- that part of transportation is gone, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you say you had a son or a daughter?

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: Son. I had a son born in June.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So he would have been a little over two years old?

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: He was, yeah. He was three years old when I got --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Three years old?

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: Well, I can't really recall.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You don't know how he reacted to --

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: I can't recall.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: He probably didn't know who you were?

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: No. Well, see, my wife lived down the street here in the double house, and my folks live on another block over here. And, of course, he spent a lot of time with my parents 'cause my wife got a job. She was working and they'd take care of him a lot. In 1949, I built this house here. We lived just about four doors down in the double house my wife and I. And we had him and then we had another little girl that was born in August of '46. She was only a couple years old. I used to wheel her back and forth, wheel her when I was up here working on this house. I saved my vacation from the post office and I had about three months off. And so consequently we had the roof on and a lot of the work done in this house when I had to go back to work. But I've had a good experience with the post office. I worked there 40 years; 22 years I carried mail. And when I went into supervision and I was an assistant at a station over here on Abbey Road for about two or three years, four years. And then I was a manager at the station for about ten years. And the last five years, I went to the main post office as superintendent. And I was in charge -- I don't know if you've ever seen our new post office over here. I was in charge of moving in the new post office. And kind of my goals were set that when I got 40 years in and I moved in a new post office, I was going to retire. So that happened. I was 62 years old. We moved in there in '81 and I retired in '82. But I still do construction. I still work at things. I built all this in here, all this stuff in here. I built all this. As the years go on, you keep changing things.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: Up on the second floor I put a -- as our family got bigger -- we have eight children. As our family got bigger, I built a dorm around the back of the house and put a bathroom up there. But now, we're putting air-conditioning upstairs I always had these room air conditioners and they're a pain in the neck really. And they didn't -- only do the room you're in. I have a friend of mine -- I'm involved with a lot of organizations that is involved with my 1937 class from Elyria High School. We graduated in '37. And he's telling me about him putting air-conditioning in his attic. And I said, hey, I can do that. So that's what these guys -- just came this morning. That's what they're up there doing now.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything else, or do you think we've covered it?

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: I think we pretty well covered -- well, there's things that come up, but I can't really think of any else.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure, yeah. An it's a unique experience, so I can't think of specific questions to ask you.

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: It was quite an experience. I still think that if you were to go back and fight in an area like that, you'd still have to use mules. I can see no way that you could ever use helicopters. If you put a piece of -- a gun down there and you wanted to take it away, you can't move it 30 feet or something like that. It can't be moved. There's no way of moving it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you become friends with the mules?

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: Well, the mules were like people. Sometimes they were temperamental and my experience was of the 15 or 16 mules that we had going -- when I was on detached service going over to C Battery, we had one mule who would never behave. I mean, it wasn't that it was nasty, he just wanted to rock. You never could control him. And what we used to do is, we'd give him the biggest load we had every day. And when that mule got into bivouac at night, his tongue was hanging out and he was ready to stand still. But if we were in that bivouac for two or three days, he'd be running around again. One time we got him -- we were going up through the jungles and he would -- it got down where one guy would -- the person was leading three mules, you know. Well, it got so confined in the jungle that we just detached them all and they could -- all they would do was follow the mule ahead of them. And this mule had to try to pass a mule where it was real narrow, and he fell over the cliff, over the side. And he fell down there about 30 feet. But we went down there, cut the cinches off of him, brought him back up, repacked him out and off we went again.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: He wasn't hurt?

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: Oh, bruised up a little bit, but he was all right. But I have another incident. I always remember the mules. We got into a place where I told you we were making this hut like. And we had to go out and get supplies. Our intentions were that we had to pack up six or eight or ten mules and make two or three trips. And we thought, why don't we get one of -- these natives had these wagons with two wheels on them, you know. Why don't we take one of those down there and take that and we can haul back all in a couple -- or get it all in one trip. Let's do it. We got around and we rigged up a harness for that -- we took one of the fella's riding mules, because we thought that was the most docile mule we had. It was just a -- it wouldn't move for nothing, really. And we put these chairs up next to it and we got a bunch of rigging and we rigged it up. And just about the time we got it all rigged up, that mule looked back and seen that shaft and it took off. It run and it run and it run. That thing was hitting trees and the wheels broke off of it. We found it about an hour later over in the jungles standing there just pooped out with one piece of wood hanging on its side yet. It was having no part of that rigging. I'll always remember that. But there's a lot of experiences that come along and you don't remember a lot of them all the time. It was an interesting trip. I thought we -- this meeting we had with this lady from Fort Bragg was supposed to come there and do some more research on these maps. I took these maps with me, but evidently she couldn't get away. She had a reservation but she never showed up. But she's doing the research on the Special Forces. 'Cause we are the origination of the Special Forces. We were just made up to go over there and get that road opened up for truck traffic. We were the originators of the Special Forces. 'Cause some of our guys were wearing these little tams now around the -- Special Forces tam, you know. But I never got any of those. This is a history of the trip to China. I don't have any more copies of this, but this was written by the officer who was in charge of taking all these -- there really was three serials of mules going to China, 300 mules in a serial. And Captain Rand was in charge of the whole outfit. And we had this Warrant Officer Blackburn who was in charge of the first serial. That's the one I was in. There were two other serials there. But we got to Kunming. But the other two serials camped out west of Kunming waiting to get into Kunming but after we got our mules there, there wasn't enough room for all of them. So they were just bivouacked out of town for a long time there. And then the war ended and we just got rid of them. But this is the story of the history of that. I ain't got no copies to give you, but . . .

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was in the New Yorker? When was that in? Do you remember? Do you have a date on that?

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: There's probably a date. November 27, 1954.

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: Yep.

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, they'll hear that and if they want to check, they can check the New Yorker.

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. I sent a copy -- I made copies of this and sent to that lady in Washington. She was appreciative of that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, very good.

sp.speaker: Earl Mahl
sp.p: Okay.
